young.html: Euripides was the youngest of the three great writers of Greek tragedy. He liked to show the old stories from a new angle: from the side of the people who lost, the women left behind, the servants, the enemies. His audiences didn't always like it, and he won the big prize only a few times. But after he died, his plays became the most popular of all.

Some of his plays have happy endings. In Alcestis, a queen agrees to die in her husband's place, and the strong hero Heracles wrestles Death himself to bring her back. In Helen, it turns out that the real Helen never went to Troy at all: the gods sent a look-alike made of cloud, while the real Helen waited in Egypt, and her husband finds her there after the war. In Iphigenia among the Taurians, a sister and brother who think each other lost meet in a faraway land and escape together.

Other plays are very sad. The Trojan Women shows the queens and princesses of Troy on the day after the city falls, waiting to learn which Greek they will be given to as captives. It asks the audience to feel the pain of the losing side.

young.html: Tell it from the other side. Pick a fairy tale you know, like "The Three Little Pigs" or "Jack and the Beanstalk". Retell it from the point of view of the wolf or the giant. Does the story change? Euripides did this with the old Greek myths.

full.html: Euripides (c. 480–406 BC) was an Athenian. A later legend says he was born on the island of Salamis on the very day of the battle there, in 480 BC. He wrote about 90 plays; 18 tragedies (one of them, Rhesus, perhaps by someone else) and one satyr play, The Cyclops, survive under his name, more than for Aeschylus and Sophocles together, partly because some of his plays were chosen for reading in schools and partly by luck. He won first prize only four times in his life. Near the end he left Athens for the court of King Archelaus of Macedon, where he died.

full.html: Medea opens with the heroine's old nurse wishing the whole story had never begun, with Jason's famous quest for the Golden Fleece:

full.text: Ah! would to Heaven the good ship Argo ne’er had sped its course to the Colchian land through the misty blue Symplegades, nor ever in the glens of Pelion the pine been felled to furnish with oars the chieftain’s hands …
full.author: Euripides
full.note: The opening of the sentence. As given in the Perseus Digital Library.

full.html: Medea, a princess of Colchis on the Black Sea, had helped Jason win the Fleece and fled with him to Greece. Now he leaves her to marry the daughter of the king of Corinth, and she is to be exiled. She takes revenge on everyone Jason loves, including, in the play's most shocking turn, their own children, and escapes in the chariot of her grandfather the Sun. The play makes Medea frightening and also lets her speak powerfully about how women, wives and foreigners were treated.

In 415 BC, the year after Athens captured the island of Melos (on the Thucydides rung), Euripides staged a play about the victims of a captured city. Hecuba, the old queen of Troy, holds the body of her little grandson, killed by the Greeks because they fear he might grow up to rebuild Troy:

full.text: What shall the bard inscribe upon your tomb about you? Argives once for fear of him slew this child? Foul shame should that inscription be to Hellas.
full.author: Euripides
full.note: As given in the Perseus Digital Library. Argives: Greeks. Hellas: Greece.

full.html: Whether the play was a protest against Melos is debated; it was probably written before or soon after. What is clear is that it asked an Athenian audience, at war, to feel for the defeated.

Gods from the machine. Euripides often ends a play with a god appearing above the stage on a crane (the mēchanē) to settle things. Later critics used the Latin phrase deus ex machina, "a god from the machine", for any too-convenient ending.

Thinking Euripides was against the gods or against women. Ancient comedians said so, and so have some modern readers. His plays let characters argue every side, often brilliantly, and leave the verdict to the audience.

deep.html: Aristotle's Poetics calls Euripides "the most tragic of the poets", even while criticizing how he built his plots. It also reports that Sophocles said he showed people as they ought to be, and Euripides as they are. Aristophanes, on the next rung, mocked him in The Frogs and other comedies as a clever talker who brought ordinary people and household matters onto the tragic stage.

Plutarch's life of the Athenian general Nicias tells that after the Athenian disaster in Sicily in 413 BC, some captured Athenians won food or even freedom by reciting Euripides, whose verses the Sicilian Greeks loved. Whether or not it is true, it shows how far his fame spread.

Medea and The Bacchae end in killings within a family, and Hippolytus turns on an unwanted love. As in all Greek tragedy, the violence happens offstage. For families, Alcestis, Helen and Iphigenia among the Taurians are good first plays.

items: Does seeing a story from the losers' side change who you think is right?
Can a character be both a victim and a villain?
Is an ending in which a god fixes everything satisfying, or a cheat?
Why might a playwright's work become more popular after his death?

questions: Euripides tells old stories from the side of the people who lost. Can you think of a book or film that does that?
In The Trojan Women, the Greeks fear that a child might grow up to take revenge. Is fear a good reason to do something?
Medea was a foreigner in Greece. How do the other characters treat her because of it?
Which ending do you prefer: one where the characters fix things themselves, or one where a god steps in?
Why do you think the Sicilians might have spared prisoners who could recite poetry?
care: Several plays center on revenge and grief, and Medea and The Bacchae include killings within a family (offstage, as always in Greek tragedy). This lesson summarizes them without detail. Alcestis, Helen and Iphigenia among the Taurians suit young readers best.
